title: Bellarmino/Perron: no asking Saints as authors of grace—absolute prayer to God alone; relative ‘pray for us’ to Saints
source_text: LII. Similiter haec est assertio Bellarmini, Non licet a Sanctis petere, ut nobis tanquam authores divinorum beneficiorum, gloriam, vel gratiam aliaque ad beatitudinem media concedant. Adeoque, juxta ipsum, nihil debemus a Sanctis petere, nisi ut a Deo impetrent quae nobis utilia sunt. De Sanct. beatitudine lib. 1. cap. 17. Cardinalis Perronius Priorem invocationem, qua aliquis invocatur, ut ipse bonorum author: orationem absolutam vocat: Posteriorem, qua aliquis rogatur, ut pro nobis oret, orationem relativam, quae scilicet, non in ipso, sed in Deo terminatur. Et priorem illam quoque soli Deo reservandam, sola vero posteriori apud Sanctos utendum docet. Adversus Regis Magnae Britanniae responsum lib. 5. cap. 1.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise this is Bellarmine’s assertion: It is not lawful to ask of the Saints that they grant us, as authors of divine benefits, glory or grace and other means to beatitude. And so, according to him, we ought to ask nothing of the Saints except that they obtain from God what is useful to us. On the Beatitude of the Saints, book 1, chapter 17. Cardinal Perron calls the former invocation, by which someone is invoked as himself the author of goods, absolute prayer: the latter, by which someone is asked to pray for us, relative prayer, which namely terminates not in him but in God. And he teaches that the former also is to be reserved to God alone, but that only the latter is to be used toward the Saints. Against the King of Great Britain’s response, book 5, chapter 1.
pass_b_english: Bellarmino: never ask Saints as authors of glory or grace—only that they obtain from God.
Perron: absolute prayer (author of goods) for God alone; relative prayer (‘pray for us’) for Saints.

choices.why: Perron’s twin terms structuring lawful Saint-invocation.
